newsitem.title: SRI LANKA: War, drought cut Sri Lanka's economic growth.
newsitem.headline: War, drought cut Sri Lanka's economic growth.

text.p: Intensified fighting has deepened Sri Lanka's woes, and the economy is set to post its worst performance in seven years, economists said on Tuesday.
Inflation has soared along with defence spending, and the arrivals of investors and tourists have plummeted.
But there is little policymakers can do. They feel straight-jacketed by the weakening economy, the economists said.
"We have revised downward our GDP growth forecast for 1996 to 3.6 percent from 4.2 percent," said Gayathri Gunaruwan of Econsult, a private economic consultancy firm.
Gross domestic product (GDP) is the total goods and services produced by an economy.
"It will be the lowest since 1989 when the leftist insurgency caused major social disruption," Gunaruwan said. GDP grew 2.3 percent in 1989.

Sri Lanka's Central Bank originally forecast GDP growth of six percent for this year against 5.5 percent growth in 1995. But hopes of achieving the 1996 forecast have been dashed by an escalation in the 14-year-old war and drought earlier this year that caused severe power shortages and crop losses.
Economists at brokerage firms Jardine Fleming and Crosby put the growth rate at 3.7 percent and 3.3 percent respectively.

The war between separatist Tamil Tiger rebels and government troops intensified when the army captured the northern rebel stronghold of Jaffna in April, but suffered its worst setback in July when the rebels overran a northeastern base, killing or capturing almost the entire garrison of 1,400 men.
The war has taken its toll on the economy. Tourist arrivals fell 31 percent to 144,648 in the first six months of 1996 compared with the same period a year earlier, the Ceylon Tourist Board said.
Industry officials said tourist arrivals plunged soon after Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam (LTTE) rebels blew up Colombo's Central Bank in January, killing almost 100 people.
Government officials said that defence spending since January had gone one-third over budget near the end of August and that the government had scaled down development projects.
Azra Jafferjee of Jardine Fleming said that worries about instability and infrastructure have turned many away investors.

"For actual foreign direct investment, we are going for $45 million this year against last year's $58 million," she said, adding that government borrowing to cover its budget deficit also hampered domestic investment.
"Had it not been for the heavy government borrowing, interest rates would have been much lower," Jafferjee said.
Sri Lanka's prime lending rate was hovering around 18 percent against the 12-month London Interbank Offered Rate (LIBOR) of around 6-7/32 percent.

Econsult said in a recent report that it was revising its forecast of end-1996 consumer price inflation to 16 percent from the earlier 12 percent because of production failure from the war, drought and the decision to end food subsidies.
August consumer prices rose 13.9 percent year-on-year.

Businessmen have asked the government to devalue the Sri Lankan rupee to boost their competitiveness in export markets. But Nanda Nair, research director at UBS Keells brokerage, said such a move could worsen inflation as Colombo tried to import military equipment and food to meet shortages caused by drought.
